checks.finding: The design explains why legacy documents remain, why facet-hybrid precedes facet-native, why DesignSync is an optional provider boundary, and why provider writes and promotion stages are deferred.
The Resolution Model, Compatibility Strategy, and Factual-Claim Reverification sections provide concrete resolution and re-check paths for the investigation questions and shared-state assumptions.
Baseline behavior claims carry checked-out commit and file/line citations, and the design requires re-verification at design review and task-decomposition planning.

The design preserves additive target selection, legacy required checks, fail-closed unknown/unrun handling, existing consent semantics, and provider-binding separation without contradicting the passed requirements or acceptance tests.

The design limits this slice to deterministic selection and contract consumers, defers runtime provider work, and identifies bounded verification-plan and host-matrix evidence rather than introducing an unbounded runtime path.
Deployment is explicitly absent for this slice; host adapters, local/CI verification, optional provider operations, and no-egress fallback are scoped with their operational boundaries.

The compatibility strategy defines the staged migration, legacy artifact retention, facet-hybrid posture, separate approval for facet-native omission, rollback-safe additive behavior, and deferred work.

Existing bootstrap, quality-loop contract checks, DesignSync, ci-mcp, host manifests, capability registry, and provider binding surfaces are identified with KEEP/PARAMETERIZE/EXTRACT/DEFER dispositions.

The bounded migration does not add provider runtime execution, cloud writes, new gate stages, package restructuring, or a second registry; target selection and compatibility boundaries are the stated scope.
The Test and Evidence Strategy names target fixtures, legacy/hybrid comparisons, consent cases, provider evidence provenance, host matrix checks, and rejection of artifact/promotion claims.
The design consistently treats capability classification as provider-neutral, bindings as provider-specific, and core approval/evidence rules as the single domain contract.
